title: Direct bounds with deferred target labels

add.label: Lemma B.2
add.name: Generic bound
add.proof:
The formula for $\varepsilon_f$ is positive since $D<q$.
The polynomial given by the formula for $E$ has quadratic coefficient $(\theta+10\varepsilon_f)/2$.
This coefficient is positive since $\theta>0$. Thus $E$ is convex.
By (P5), $E(2)\le 2^{-\lambda}$.
Adding the two inequalities of (P5) gives $E(2^{\lambda+1})\le 1$.
The affine function $u/2^{\lambda+1}$ takes those upper bounds at the two endpoints.
Convexity bounds $E$ by this affine function on $[2,2^{\lambda+1}]$.
Taking $u=2Q+2$ gives the claim.
add.explain: Proves the bound used on the outgoing edge.

add.name: Heavy stacks
add.label: Lemma B.8
add.statement:
Let the parameters satisfy (P3), and let $\mathbf{W}$ be a heavy stack.

 
(a) $\operatorname{rank} \mathbf{W} \le 3$.
(b) Every kernel vector $v$ in the row space of $\mathbf{W}$ has a short multiple.
(c) If $x$ is a short multiple of a kernel vector, then $\hat x \in R^\ell$, with the $\hat x_j$ of Definition 5.1 over $\mathbb{Z}$, solves MSIS for the matrix $A$ of the columns $1, \dots, \ell$ of $M$ (Definition 3.3): $0 < \|\hat x\|_\infty \le \beta$ and $A \hat x = 0 \bmod q$.
add.explain: Directly counts stack fibers and applies the inverse theorem to the kernel vector.
add.proof:
Suppose the matrix formed by stacking the rows of the $W_c$ has rank at least four.
Choose four independent columns including column $0$ if it is nonzero.
Fix the independent draws corresponding to the other columns, with $r_\star$ corresponding to column $0$ in $\mathcal D_g$.
If column $0$ is unchosen, it is zero.
A fiber prescribes at most one residue tuple in the four chosen columns by their independence.
The residues at the chosen nonzero indices determine at most one draw each since $g<q$.
If column $0$ was chosen, its residue determines at most one independent draw, since in $\mathcal D_g$ the remaining entries now fix the shift from $r_\star$.
Each fiber therefore contains at most a fraction $g^{-4}$ of the draws.
Condition (I5) gives $g^{-4}<\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The definition $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}=\theta-100\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ gives $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}<\theta$ since $\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}>0$.
This fiber bound contradicts heaviness.

Let $v$ be a kernel vector in the row space.
The constant coefficient of $z(v)=0$ gives $v_0=0$.
As $v$ lies in the row space, $v^\top r$ is constant on each stack fiber.
The heaviest fiber then gives $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)\ge\operatorname{gp}(\mathbf W)$.
Heaviness gives $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$.
The incoming inverse bound supplies a short multiple.

For any short multiple $x$, its reduction lies in the kernel of $z$ by linearity.
The constant coefficient then gives $x_0=0\bmod q$.
The bound $|x_0|\le\beta<q$ implies $x_0=0$ over the integers.
The remaining coefficients of $z(x\bmod q)$ are those of $A\hat x$ by the definition of the forms at $x_0=0$.
Thus $A\hat x=0\bmod q$.
The short multiple has nonzero reduction, so $x\ne 0$. 
Packing $x_1,\dots,x_N$ with zero padding preserves $0<\|x\|_\infty\le\beta$.

add.label: Lemma 4.7
add.name: QAP criterion by coset averaging
add.explain: Uses simultaneous divisibility and the root bound on the coset average.
add.statement:
For admissible evaluation points and symmetric $W$, passing is equivalent to divisibility of $P_W-Z_0R$ by $Z$ for an allowed $R$.
Passing is also equivalent to divisibility of $P_W-\chi L_\rho-Z_0R$ by $Z(X)(X-\rho)$ for an allowed $R$ and a scalar $\chi$.
The respective quotients have degrees below $D$ and $D-1$.
Both divisions require $R=R_W$, and the second requires $\chi=W_{00}$. For a witness $w$, both divisions exist for $W=ww^\top$ with $\chi=1$.
add.proof:
By the QAP table, $P_W-Z_0R$ vanishes on $\mathcal P_0\setminus\{\rho\}$ exactly when the Booleanity tests hold.
On the cosets, vanishing requires exactly the interpolant $R_W$ because $R$ has degree below $\nu n_{\mathsf c}$.
The factor theorem therefore gives divisibility by $Z$ exactly when the Booleanity tests hold and $R=R_W$.
By the QAP table, passing the constraints means that the coset sums of $R_W$ vanish.
The polynomial $\sum_{\xi\in\mathcal G}R_W(\xi X)$ takes those sums at all $\nu n_{\mathsf c}$ coset points.
It vanishes at those points exactly when it is zero by its degree bound.
The monomial sum rule shows that it is zero exactly when $R_W$ has no exponent divisible by $\nu$, since $\nu\ne0$ in $\mathbb F_q$.
Thus the interpolant is allowed exactly when the constraint tests hold.
Interpolation gives $L_\rho=Z/Z(\rho)$.
Subtracting $\chi L_\rho$ therefore preserves divisibility by $Z$ in both directions.
The QAP table gives $P_W(\rho)-\chi L_\rho(\rho)-Z_0(\rho)R(\rho)=W_{00}-\chi$.
Given divisibility by $Z$, the factor theorem makes the extra factor $X-\rho$ equivalent to $\chi=W_{00}$.
The degrees of the numerators are at most $2D-2$ by the defining degrees.
Subtracting the respective divisor degrees gives the two bounds.
A witness $w$ has $w_0=1$, which gives $(ww^\top)_{00}=1$.
On its moment matrix, the Booleanity tests give $w_j^2-w_j=0$.
Each constraint test gives $\sum_f a_{t,f}(w)b_{t,f}(w)-w_0c_t(w)=0$ by the witness property.
Thus both divisions exist by the equivalences.

add.label: Lemma B.6
add.name: A witness in the row space
add.explain: Uses the symmetric trilinear form forced by the ties and the Boolean coordinates.
add.statement: A nonzero usable stack of rank at most three with no kernel vector in its row space has a witness of $S$ in that row space.
add.proof:
Let $\mathcal V$ be the row space of the stack and $d$ its dimension.
Take a basis matrix $\mathcal U$ for $\mathcal V$ with rows $u_i$.
Construct $h_s$ by evaluating $\sigma^s(z)$ on the chosen basis, for $s=0,n/2-1,n/2,n/2+1$.
The entries of $h_0$ are independent over $\mathbb F_q$ because a nonzero combination of the basis vectors cannot belong to the kernel of $z$.
The basis vectors are over $\mathbb F_q$, so $h_s=\sigma^s(h_0)$.
The field automorphism preserves independence of the entries.
The first $d$ consecutive columns from $h_{n/2-1}$ form a basis by the Moore determinant.
The matrices $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ are symmetric because the stack matrices are symmetric.
Their columns belong to the extension-field span of $\mathcal U$ because each is a combination of stack matrices.
Apply a left inverse of $\mathcal U$ to the three matrices on the left and its transpose on the right to obtain $\Xi_{n/2-1},\Xi_{n/2},\Xi_{n/2+1}$, respectively.
Multiplying these by $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal U^\top$ reconstructs $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ because their column and row spaces lie in the chosen span.
These coordinate matrices are symmetric by applying the same left inverse on both sides, transposed on the right.
Reconstruction by $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal U^\top$ is injective because $\mathcal U$ has a left inverse.
Modulo $P$, the substitutions $-T/\omega,-T,-\omega T$ are the corresponding powers of $\sigma$ by $\omega^{n/2}=-1$.
The three tie equations then give $\Xi_s h_{s'}=\Xi_{s'}h_s$ in row-space coordinates.
For the tie equations and linear extension let $s,s'$ range over $n/2-1,n/2,n/2+1$.
Any relation $\sum_s\varrho_s h_s=0$ implies $(\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s)h_{s'}=0$ for each $s'$ by the ties.
Thus $\sum_s\varrho_s\Xi_s=0$ because the $h_{s'}$ span.
Consequently $h_s\mapsto\Xi_s$ extends to a linear map $\Xi$.
Its trilinear form $\Xi(h;u,u')=u^\top\Xi(h)u'$ is symmetric in its last two inputs.
The ties give symmetry in its first and last inputs on spanning vectors.
Hence it is symmetric in all three inputs.
The form is nonzero because $W_U,W_V$ together contain all coefficients of the nonzero stack.
All three matrices obey the Booleanity tests by linearity of those tests over the extension field.
Those tests give $\Xi(h_s;u_j,u_j-u_0)=0$ for every $j\in[N]$.
By linearity these equations hold with every $h$ in place of $h_s$.
The even exponents of $W_V$ give $W_V=\sigma^{n/2}(W_V)$.
The identity $\sigma^n=\mathrm{id}$ gives $W_U=\sigma^{n/2-1}(\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U))$.
Since $\mathcal U$ is over $\mathbb F_q$, these equalities give $\Xi_s=\sigma^s(\Xi_{n-s})$ for $s\in\{n/2-1,n/2\}$.

If $u_0=0$, choose a basis $l_1,\dots,l_d$ among the other rows.
Booleanity and symmetry make every basis entry with a repeated index zero.
A nonzero entry then requires $d=3$.
By symmetry the entries on permutations of the distinct indices all equal $\Xi(l_1;l_2,l_3)$.
In this basis $\Xi(h_s;l_b,l_c)$ for distinct $b,c$ is $\Xi(l_1;l_2,l_3)$ times the coordinate of $h_s$ at the remaining $l_a$.
Comparing these entries in the Frobenius equalities gives $\Xi(l_1;l_2,l_3)h_s=\sigma^s(\Xi(l_1;l_2,l_3))h_0$ since $\sigma^s(h_{n-s})=h_0$.
For $\Xi(l_1;l_2,l_3)\ne0$ both $h_{n/2-1}$ and $h_{n/2}$ are multiples of $h_0$.
This contradicts their independence in the Moore basis.
Thus $u_0\ne0$.

Complete $l_0=u_0$ to a basis $l_0,\dots,l_{d-1}$ using other rows.
For each $\delta\in\{0,1\}^{d-1}$ let $p_\delta$ be the unique vector over $\mathbb F_q$ with evaluations $(1,\delta)$ on this basis.
Define $w_\delta=\mathcal U p_\delta$.
By symmetry and Booleanity, a basis entry of $\Xi$ depends only on its set of positive indices, since one occurrence of a repeated positive index can be replaced by $0$.
The cubic evaluation tensor of $p_\delta$ on a basis triple is one exactly when its set of positive indices lies in the support of $\delta$.
Inclusion ordering makes this incidence matrix triangular with diagonal one.
Consequently $\Xi(h)=\sum_\delta c_\delta(h^\top p_\delta)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ for extension-field coefficients $c_\delta$.
The matrix of the $p_\delta p_\delta^\top$ evaluated on basis pairs has the same incidence rows, since every subset of positive indices occurs on a pair for $d-1\le2$.
Hence these squares are linearly independent.
The absence of kernel vectors gives $z(w_\delta)\ne0$ since $(w_\delta)_0=1$.
The expansion gives $\Xi_s=\sum_\delta c_\delta\sigma^s(z(w_\delta))p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
Comparing square coefficients in the Frobenius equalities gives $c_\delta\sigma^s(z(w_\delta))=\sigma^s(c_\delta)z(w_\delta)$ for $s\in\{n/2-1,n/2\}$.
Thus $c_\delta/z(w_\delta)$ is fixed by both consecutive powers.
It is fixed by $\sigma$ by composing one power with the inverse of the other.
Write $c_\delta=\chi_\delta z(w_\delta)$ with $\chi_\delta\in\mathbb F_q$.

Every linear test $\varrho$ vanishes on $W_U,W_V,\sigma^{n/2+1}(W_U)$ because all $W_c$ pass.
Let $\mathcal Q=\sum_\delta\chi_\delta\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)p_\delta p_\delta^\top$.
The coordinate expansions then give $h_0^\top\mathcal Q h_s=0$ for each of the three consecutive $h_s$.
Hence $h_0^\top\mathcal Q=0$ because the $h_s$ span.
The independence of the entries of $h_0$ makes $\mathcal Q=0$, since $\mathcal Q$ is over $\mathbb F_q$.
Independence of the squares gives $\chi_\delta\varrho(w_\delta w_\delta^\top)=0$ for every $\delta$.
Some $\chi_\delta$ is nonzero because $\Xi$ is nonzero.
For this $\delta$ all tests of $w_\delta w_\delta^\top$ pass.
The Booleanity tests give $(w_\delta)_j^2=(w_\delta)_j$ at each coordinate because $(w_\delta)_0=1$.
The constraint tests give the quadratic constraints because each term on this matrix factors into its two evaluations at $w_\delta$.
Each solution of $(w_\delta)_j^2=(w_\delta)_j$ lies in $\{0,1\}$ because $\mathbb F_q$ is a field.
Thus $w_\delta$ is a witness in $\mathcal V$.

add.label: Lemma B.7
add.name: A short vector from a dense fiber
add.explain: Constructs low-rank prefix lattices and takes a short point in their projected line preimage.
add.statement: Under (I1) to (I6) for prime $q$, every nonzero $v\in\mathbb F_q^{N+1}$ with $v_0=0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$ has a short multiple $x$ with $x_0=0$.
add.proof:
Discard the zero coordinates of $v$, keeping the nonzero coordinates in the order $v_1,\dots,v_{N_0}$.
The sampler draws in those coordinates independently and uniformly by its definition.
The discarded coordinates contribute zero to the linear form.
Conditioning on the next independent draw shifts the preceding linear form by a constant.
Averaging the point masses gives $\operatorname{gp}(v_{[i]}^\top)\ge\operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top)$.
The first coordinate has guessing probability $1/g$ since multiplication by $v_1$ is injective on the box.
Every prefix therefore has guessing probability above $\theta$.

For each prefix, construct a regular saturated lattice $\Theta$ of rank $d\in[3]$ with $v_{[i]}\in\bar\Theta$ and $m(\Theta)>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
At length one use $\mathbb Z$, whose reduction is all of $\mathbb F_q$.
It has height one.
Its point fibers have density $1/g$.
This density exceeds $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ because $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}<\theta<1/g$.
Now (I4) gives $\Gamma_1^{b-1}>1$.
Hence $\mathbb Z$ is regular.
For ranks one and two, regularity yields $h(\Theta)\le H_d$.
For rank three this height bound is the incoming dense-prefix conclusion.

Choose a largest minor $J$ of $\Theta$.
The largest-minor demand makes restriction to $J$ injective.
The projected lattice has determinant $h(\Theta)$ by the minor formula.
Apply the incoming Minkowski and Mahler basis-product bound to the projection in the one-norm.
It gives a basis with product of lengths at most $h(\Theta),2h(\Theta),9h(\Theta)$ in ranks one, two and three respectively.
Pull that basis back along the injective projection, obtaining a basis matrix $B$.
The largest-minor coordinate bound gives the same bounds for the product of its column sup norms.

The induction property gives $v_{[i]}=Bc'\bmod q$ for some $c'$.
Let $c=(c',v_{i+1})$.
The map $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_{[i]},r_{i+1})$ satisfies $c^\top\Phi(r)=v_{[i+1]}^\top r\bmod q$.
Trim a densest modular fiber of the latter form by $\Theta$, calling the result $F$.
The trimming demand gives $\Pr[F]\ge\operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top)-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The image $\Phi(F)$ lies in an index-$q$ coset because $v_{i+1}\ne0$.
If it had full dimension, the sparsity bound would give $\Pr[F]\le\Lambda_d g^d h(\Theta)m(\Theta)/q$.
Regularity bounds this by $\Lambda_d\Gamma_d/q$.
By (I5) that bound is below $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
The fiber lower bound is above $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by $\operatorname{gp}(v_{[i+1]}^\top)>\theta$.
Let $\Delta$ have all pairwise differences of points of $\Phi(F)$ as columns.
Its rank is at most $d$ by the affine dimension bound.

The trimming ellipsoid bounds differences in coordinate $j\in[d]$ of $B^\top r_{[i]}$ by $2R_{\mathrm{tr}}\sqrt{(\Sigma_\Theta)_{jj}}$ by Cauchy--Schwarz.
The covariance formula bounds this by $T_{\mathrm{tr}}\|Be_j\|_\infty$.
By (I2), $T_{\mathrm{tr}}\ge g$.
This also bounds differences in the last box coordinate.
The determinant expansion bounds each maximal minor of $\Delta$ by $d!T_{\mathrm{tr}}^d\prod_{j=1}^d\|Be_j\|_\infty$, since the column norms and $T_{\mathrm{tr}}$ are at least one.
The basis bound and the height bound turn this into at most $H_1T_{\mathrm{tr}},4H_2T_{\mathrm{tr}}^2$, or $54H_3T_{\mathrm{tr}}^3$.
Each is below $q$ by (I5).
Since $c^\top\Delta=0\bmod q$, the modular lifting demand gives an integer $u\equiv c\bmod q$ with $u^\top\Delta=0$.
Thus $u^\top\Phi(r)$ is constant on $F$.
The formula for $\Phi$ puts $(Bu_{[d]},u_{d+1})$ in $F^\perp$.
Its reduction is $v_{[i+1]}$ by $u\equiv c\bmod q$.
This proves $v_{[i+1]}\in\overline{F^\perp}$.
This also makes the normal lattice nonzero.
Its largest fiber density is at least $\Pr[F]$ by definition of the normal lattice.
The rank is at most three by the fiber-density bound and $\Pr[F]>\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}>g^{-4}$.
The density is greater than $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ by the trimming bound and the definition of $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Regularization gives a regular saturated superlattice of rank at most three at a density loss of at most $2\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
Its density is above $\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
It retains the reduction of $v_{[i+1]}$ by inclusion.

Take a basis matrix $B$ and largest minor $J$ at the final length.
Choose $z_0\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $Bz_0=v_{[N_0]}\bmod q$ by the induction property.
The residue of $z_0$ is nonzero since $v_{[N_0]}$ is nonzero.
The integer vectors reducing to the line of $z_0$ have index $q^{d-1}$.
Their images under $B_J$ form a lattice of determinant $h(\Theta)q^{d-1}$.
By (I6) and the height bounds, $d!h(\Theta)q^{d-1}\le\beta^d$, using that the height is integral when $d=3$.
The one-norm ball of radius $\beta$ then has volume at least $2^d h(\Theta)q^{d-1}$.
Minkowski gives a nonzero point $B_Jz$ in that ball.
The coordinate bound yields $\|Bz\|_\infty\le\beta$.
The lift $Bz$ is nonzero because $B_Jz$ is nonzero.
Its reduction is nonzero because its sup norm is at most $\beta<q$.
By construction that reduction is a multiple of $v_{[N_0]}$.
Restoring the discarded coordinates as zeros gives the desired short multiple.

add.label: Lemma B.17
add.name: Integer lattices
add.explain: Uses the largest minor for coordinate control and the Chinese remainder theorem to lift a modular relation.
add.statement:
For a lattice $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb Z^I$ with a largest minor at $J$, the restriction to $J$ is injective on $\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(\Theta)$ and $|y_i|\le\|y_J\|_1$ for every $y$ in that span and $i\in I$.
For prime $q$, if an integer matrix $\Delta$ with row set $I$ has rank $k$ and all $k\times k$ minors have absolute value below $q$, every $c\in\mathbb Z^I$ with $c^\top\Delta=0\bmod q$ is congruent modulo $q$ to an integer $u$ with $u^\top\Delta=0$.
add.proof:
Take a basis matrix $B$ for $\Theta$.
Cramer's rule expresses each row of $B$ in the rows of $B_J$ with coefficients given by ratios of minors to $\det B_J$.
Every coefficient has absolute value at most one by maximality of the minor.
For $y$ in the column span of $B$, the same row combination expresses $y_i$ in the entries of $y_J$.
The triangle inequality gives $|y_i|\le\|y_J\|_1$.
Thus vanishing at $J$ implies vanishing everywhere.

For rank zero take $u=c$.
Otherwise choose a nonzero $k\times k$ minor of $\Delta$.
Its determinant is coprime to $q$ by the minor bound.
For rows outside this minor, choose the entries of $u$ congruent to those of $c$ modulo $q$ and divisible by the determinant using the Chinese remainder theorem.
Solve the equations $u^\top\Delta=0$ on the selected columns for the selected row entries.
The right sides are divisible by the determinant by the outer coordinate choices.
Cramer's rule makes the solution integral.
The selected row entries reduce to those of $c$ by uniqueness of the solution modulo $q$.
The selected columns span the rational column space by the rank-$k$ minor criterion.
The relation on the selected columns therefore holds on every column.

add.label: Proposition B.15
add.name: Reduction time from circuit records
add.explain: Counts deferred label assignments and differentiates the arithmetic circuit of records.
add.statement: Under the hypotheses of Theorem 5.9, for adversary time $t$ and at most $Q_H$ queries to each random oracle, both reductions run within $t_R=t+O(Q+d_R Q_H+\mu)+\mathsf{poly}(D,\log q)$ in the stated operations model including description and advice.
add.proof:
Keep both directions of the injection in tables, with flags for rejected strings.
When testing operands, the generators already occupy strings, so each undecided count is below $2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}}$.
By exchangeability, an undecided string is valid with probability equal to the unused exponent count divided by the undecided count.
Sample validity by the corresponding uniform integer threshold test.
A new valid string receives a uniform unused exponent.
A new exponent receives a uniform undecided string.
Each call uses at most two operand tests and one result assignment.
Check the received-label flag on a name request.
Use the negative exponent for the other label of an eligible name request.
Table updates and field arithmetic therefore cost $O(Q)$ operations.

Keep each record as a circuit root, using zero for an operand without a record.
A linear operation, pairing or negation appends a constant number of gates.
Evaluate each new gate also at the independently sampled private point.
Retain the first pair of roots for a result in $\mathbb G_T$ and its existing record with unequal private values.
Each label keeps its first record.
The other root for (R3) is the target label's stored record if present.
Represent $G_T$ by the pairing of the generators.
Treat $G_2$ as a plain-sector leaf.
For each recovery point, zero the other sector's right-group leaves.
In the plain sector zero the key leaf.
This gives the selected sector by the target expression formula.
The gradient theorem differentiates that circuit in $O(Q+L)$ operations with respect to its leaves.
In the raw right factor only the first coordinate depends on $r_j$.
The first column of $\Omega^{-1}$ is $(1,0)^\top$.
Thus this dependence stays in the first published coordinate and its alpha copy.
The chain rule therefore adds each leaf derivative to at most one search-coordinate derivative at constant cost.
The number of recovery points and tested expressions is bounded by (R2) and (R3).
Elimination for (R5) uses vectors of length $N+1$ and $n$ form equations.
Elimination costs polynomial time in $D$.
At most two lifts cost polynomial time in $N$ and $\log q$ by the lifting demand.

The publication index ranges are polynomial in $D$ by $N,n\le D$, $K_1K_2=n/2$, $J\Delta\le D+n$ and the remainder chunk definitions.
The eight tuples are sampled coordinatewise from the specified sets with polynomial-size exclusion lists.
The centered sampler computes $r_0$ by one sum and the indicated rounding.
Evaluate published exponents at the encryption, private and recovery points by field arithmetic and ordinary ring convolution.
Their formulas and polynomial-sized index ranges give polynomial cost in $D$ and $\log q$.
Hardwire the QAP coefficients as advice of polynomial size since their degrees are at most $D$.
Preload the seed table with the challenge coefficients.
A new seed reply uses $d_R$ independent uniform field samples.
Draw each new key reply independently and uniformly in its output set.
Reuse the stored reply on repeated inputs.
Table lookups and insertions with references to those values cost $O(d_R Q_H)$ for the queries.
The mask and advice for the message cost $O(\mu)$ in writes and XORs.
Adding these costs to $t$ gives the time bound.

add.label: Lemma B.13
add.name: A guessed target label
add.statement: The probability that the first mark is $\mathsf{guess}$ is at most $2^\lambda/N_{\mathsf{free}}$.
add.explain: Bounds the first guessed target before its assignment.
add.proof:
In $\mathsf{R}_m$, sample the uniform mask first.
Set the target oracle value to the mask XOR $m$.
This changes no answer in $\mathsf{R}_\$$ before the first target query.
The first mark is decided by that query by (M4).
Lazy sampling decides at most $2+3Q$ $\mathbb G_T$ strings from received labels, operands and results.
Every assigned label has an entry before the first mark by (M1)–(M3).
By (M4), a first $\mathsf{guess}$ hits an unassigned target.
In $\mathsf{R}_\$$, the other coins and prior $\mathsf{lab}_T$ decisions fix each query.
By symmetry an unassigned target label is uniform over undecided strings.
Their count is at least $2^{\ell_{\mathsf{lab}}}-2-3Q\ge N_{\mathsf{free}}$.
Summing the conditional hit bound $1/N_{\mathsf{free}}$ over $Q_H\le2^\lambda$ queries proves the claim.

edges.demand: Under (I1) to (I6) for prime $q$, every nonzero $v$ with $v_0=0$ and $\operatorname{gp}(v^\top)>\theta$ has an integer $x$ with $\|x\|_\infty\le\beta$, $x_0=0$ and $x\equiv c v\pmod q$ for some $c\ne0$.
X^k sums over a coset of order ν to ν·δ^k if ν divides k, and to zero otherwise.
The Moore determinant of elements that are linearly independent over F_q is nonzero.

For a largest minor at $J$, restriction to $J$ is injective on the real lattice span and $|y_i|\le\|y_J\|_1$. For prime $q$, a modular left relation on an integer matrix of rank $k$ with all $k\times k$ minors of absolute value below $q$ lifts to an integer left relation with the same residues.
For a saturated lattice $\Theta$ of rank three with $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}$, $h(\Theta)\le H_3$.
Trimming costs at most ε_(tr) of density.

Let $\Theta$ have rank $d\in[3]$ on at most $N$ coordinates and basis $B$. For a nonempty box set $F$ on those and one additional coordinate $i\prime$, trimmed by $\Theta$, put $\Phi(r)=(B^\top r_I,r_{i\prime})$. If $\dim\Phi(F)=d+1$ and $\Phi(F)$ is in a coset of an index-$q$ subgroup of $\mathbb Z^{d+1}$, then $\Pr[F]\le\Lambda_d g^d h(\Theta)m(\Theta)/q$.

A saturated lattice $\Theta\subseteq\mathbb Z^I$ with $|I|\le N$, rank $d\in[3]$ and $m(\Theta)\ge\mu_{\mathrm{tr}}+(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$ is contained in a regular saturated lattice of rank in $[d,3]$ and density at least $m(\Theta)-(3-d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{tr}}$.
A lattice of rank d has fiber density at most g^(−d).
A symmetric convex body of volume 2^d·det contains a nonzero lattice point: the short multiple.
Minkowski's second theorem and Mahler's lemma: a basis whose norms have product at most h, 2h or 9h.
T_(LIFT) is polynomial in N and log q.
Sampling the reduction's coins before the run changes no output.
The gradient of a computation costs a constant number of operations per operation of the computation.
Lazy sampling of the label map of G_T.

discharge.argument: The statement directly supplies the bound under (P5) for the stated query range.
Clauses (a), (b), and (c) give the rank bound, existence of a short multiple for a kernel vector of the row space, and the Module-SIS property of its packing.
Clause (a) supplies rank at most three.
The identities give the corresponding divisibility with an allowed remainder. Both directions give passing, and the key-cell divisibility forces its corner to be chi.
The witness clause gives both exact divisions with unit key coefficient, and the general conclusion gives the allowed remainder and respective degree bounds.
The statement supplies exactly the witness conclusion at rank at most three under nonzero usability and absence of a kernel vector.
